interview.answer: A keyword added to a selector that targets an element in a particular state or position, such as :hover or :first-child.

interview.q: How does a pseudo-class differ from a pseudo-element in CSS?
interview.answer: A pseudo-class filters existing elements by state; a pseudo-element generates or targets a sub-part of an element.
It matches when the user's pointer is over the element.
It matches when the element has keyboard or programmatic focus.

interview.q: Why prefer :focus-visible over :focus for form controls?
interview.answer: It shows a focus ring for keyboard users while avoiding it on mouse clicks.
It matches an element that contains a focused descendant.
It matches while the element is being activated, such as during a mouse press.
It matches links the user has already visited, with strict styling limits for privacy.
To prevent scripts from reading visited links through computed styles, which would leak browsing history.
Checked checkboxes, radio buttons and selected option elements.
Form controls that are disabled and cannot be interacted with.
Form controls that are not disabled.
Form controls with the required attribute.
Form controls without the required attribute.
Form controls whose value satisfies their validation constraints.
Form controls whose value fails validation.
Inputs whose value is within the min and max range.
Inputs whose value is outside the min and max range.
Inputs currently showing their placeholder text.
An element that is the first child of its parent.
An element that is the last child of its parent.
It matches children by position using a formula such as 2n+1 for odd children.

interview.q: What is the difference between :nth-child and :nth-of-type?
interview.answer: :nth-child counts all siblings; :nth-of-type counts only siblings of the same element type.

interview.q: When is :only-child useful in component styling?
interview.answer: It styles an element differently when it has no siblings, such as a lone list item.
An element with no children, including no text nodes.
:not() excludes matching elements, while :is() and :where() include them.
It matches any element matching one of the listed selectors, with the specificity of the most specific argument.
Like :is() but with zero specificity, useful for low-specificity defaults.
It matches an element that has a descendant or sibling matching the given selector, enabling parent selection.

interview.q: Why is :has() called the parent selector?
interview.answer: Because it lets you style a parent based on its children, which was previously impossible in CSS.
It counts children from the end instead of the beginning.
It counts siblings of the same type from the end.
The first sibling of its element type within its parent.
The last sibling of its element type within its parent.
An element that is the only sibling of its type within its parent.
It matches the document root element, usually html, and is often used for CSS variables.
It matches the element whose id matches the URL fragment.
It matches elements based on their language attribute or inherited language.
It matches elements based on text direction, such as ltr or rtl.
The default option in a select or the default submit button in a form.
Checkboxes or radio buttons in an indeterminate state, or progress elements.
Form controls that cannot be edited, such as those with readonly.
Form controls that can be edited.
The specificity of its most specific argument, which can make it unexpectedly strong.
Zero, so it never increases specificity.
